title: The Trial Before Pilate, the Cross, and the Burial
summary: The council brings Jesus to Pilate on political charges. Pilate finds no basis for them, sends Jesus to Herod Antipas, and three times declares him innocent, but under the crowd's pressure releases the insurrectionist Barabbas and hands Jesus over to be crucified. On the cross Jesus prays for those who crucify him, promises paradise to a repentant criminal, and commits his spirit to the Father. A centurion calls him righteous, and Joseph of Arimathea buries him in a new tomb while the women from Galilee watch.
story: This chapter is the lowest point of Luke's story and, as the Gospel will show, its turning point. Everything Jesus foretold on the road to Jerusalem now happens: he is handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, and killed (18:32-33). Luke stresses again and again that Jesus is innocent. Pilate says so three times, Herod finds nothing, the criminal on the cross says so, and the centurion says so at the end. Yet the innocent one dies alongside the guilty, and a guilty man goes free in his place. The women who followed from Galilee see where he is buried, which matters for the next chapter: they will know which tomb is empty.
historical:
Pontius Pilate was the Roman prefect of Judea from AD 26 to 36. An inscription found at Caesarea in 1961 bears his name and title. Jewish writers of the first century, Philo and Josephus, describe him as stubborn and harsh, and Luke himself mentions Galileans whose blood Pilate mixed with their sacrifices (13:1). The charges brought to him were chosen to matter to Rome: subverting the nation, opposing taxes to Caesar, and claiming to be a king. Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea as tetrarch from about 4 BC to AD 39. He was the Herod who executed John the Baptist, and Luke alone records Jesus' appearance before him.

Crucifixion was the Roman punishment for slaves, rebels, and the lowest criminals, designed to be public, slow, and shameful. Victims were often flogged first, made to carry the crossbeam, and fixed to the cross with nails or ropes, and a placard stated the charge. Death could take hours or days. The place called The Skull (Golgotha in Aramaic, Calvary from the Latin) lay just outside the city walls; the Church of the Holy Sepulchre marks the site tradition has identified since the fourth century. Tombs cut into rock, with a bench for the body and a stone to close the entrance, have been found in large numbers around Jerusalem.
cultural:
Simon of Cyrene came from a city in North Africa (modern Libya) with a large Jewish community; Mark names his sons, Alexander and Rufus, as though his readers knew them. Roman soldiers could compel civilians to carry loads. Women publicly mourning a condemned man were doing something risky, and Jesus turns their grief toward the suffering coming on the city, quoting Hosea 10:8. His saying about green and dry wood is a proverb: if they treat the innocent this way, what will happen to the guilty.

The soldiers dividing his clothes was a customary perk of executioners, and Luke's wording echoes Psalm 22:18. The sour wine offered by the soldiers was the cheap wine that soldiers drank. The hours are counted from sunrise, so the sixth hour is about noon and the ninth about three in the afternoon. The temple curtain most likely refers to the veil that separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place. Jewish custom required burial before nightfall, especially before a Sabbath, and Romans often left the crucified unburied as a final humiliation, though in Judea bodies were at times released for burial. Joseph's request to Pilate was a bold act for a council member.
literary: Luke tells the passion in a sequence of scenes: Pilate, Herod, Pilate again, the road, the cross, the death, and the burial. Repetition carries his emphasis. Pilate's verdict of innocence comes three times (verses 4, 14 to 15, 22), and three groups mock Jesus at the cross (the rulers, the soldiers, and one criminal) with the same taunt: save yourself. The irony is that Jesus is saving others precisely by not saving himself. Jesus speaks three times on the cross in Luke, and all three sayings are unique to Luke: the prayer for forgiveness, the promise to the criminal, and the final prayer from Psalm 31:5. Verse 34a, the prayer for forgiveness, is missing from some early manuscripts, but many scholars accept it, and it matches Stephen's prayer in Acts 7:60. Verse 17 is absent from the earliest manuscripts.

doctrines.note: Luke's story shows substitution in action: Barabbas, guilty of insurrection and murder, is released, and Jesus, declared innocent three times, dies in his place. The innocent one is numbered with the transgressors, as Jesus said Scripture required (22:37).

The criminal on the cross has no time to do anything but confess his guilt, recognize Jesus' innocence, and ask to be remembered. Jesus promises him paradise that same day. Salvation is received, not earned.

The chapter is full of human decisions (the council's, Pilate's, Herod's, the crowd's), and Luke holds them responsible. Yet the Gospel and Acts both present these events as fulfilling what God had determined (22:22, Acts 2:23). Human evil does not defeat God's purpose.

words.note: Paradeisos, paradise. The word came into Greek from Persian, where it meant an enclosed park or garden. The Septuagint uses it for the garden of Eden, and in later Jewish writing it named the place of the righteous dead. Jesus promises the criminal, “today you will be with Me in Paradise”, a restored Eden in his company.

Dikaios, righteous or just, innocent. The centurion's words, “Surely this was a righteous man”, sum up Luke's emphasis on Jesus' innocence. The word also echoes the righteous sufferer of the Psalms and the righteous servant of Isaiah 53:11, who bears the iniquities of many.

Katapetasma, curtain or veil. In the Septuagint it names the curtain before the Most Holy Place, where God's presence dwelt and where only the high priest entered once a year. Its tearing at Jesus' death is read in Hebrews 10:19-20 as the opening of a new way into God's presence, though interpreters also see in it a sign of judgment on the temple.

christ: The cross is the center of the Christian confession, and Luke shows who is dying on it. He is the King of the Jews, as the inscription says in mockery and as the reader knows in truth. He is the Christ of God, the Chosen One, as the rulers sneer. He is the righteous one who prays for his executioners, opens paradise to a dying criminal, and entrusts his spirit to his Father with the words of a psalm. His death fulfills Isaiah's servant, who was numbered with transgressors and bore the sin of many. The church confesses that here, in this public, shameful Roman execution, the Son of God gave his life for sinners, and that this death, far from being the end of the story, is the means by which God saves.

hard.q: Who was responsible for the death of Jesus, and has this chapter been misused?
hard.a: Luke names many participants: Judas, the chief priests and council, Herod, Pilate, the soldiers, and a crowd in Jerusalem. Historically, crucifixion was a Roman punishment, and only the Roman governor could order it. Luke's emphasis on Pilate's reluctance has led some historians to suspect that Luke softens Roman responsibility; others note that Pilate still gave the order and that his three declarations of innocence make his decision all the more damning. Tragically, passages like this were used for centuries to blame the Jewish people as a whole for Jesus' death, a charge that fueled persecution. The text does not support it. Jesus and his followers were Jews, the women of Jerusalem mourn him, many of the people go home grieving, and a member of the council buries him. Christian theology has long insisted that the deepest cause of Jesus' death is the sin of all humanity, and that he laid down his life willingly. The prayer, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,” is the answer the cross itself gives to the question of blame.

questions: Pilate knew Jesus was innocent and handed him over anyway. Where are you tempted to do what you know is wrong because of pressure from others?
The criminal on the cross brought nothing but an honest confession and a request. What does his story say to someone who thinks it is too late?
Jesus prayed for those who were killing him. Whom would you find it hardest to pray for in that way?
